July 23, 1972
Director
Bureau of Outdoor Recreation
Pepartment of the Interior
Washington, D.C. 20515
Re.: Int DES 72-62
Dear Sir:
Indiana Sassafras Audubon opposes the establishment of motorized vehicle trails in national forests. We feel there is no reason that national forests have to consider ORVs as an important recreational asset in the forest land.
Our opinions are based on close observation of the controversy in our own National Hoosier Forest, participation at a hike conducted by the Forest Service on July 15, 1972 (see enclosed newspaper clipping) in the Hickory Ridge Area near Monroe Reservoir, and the Draft Environmental Analysis, proposed Off Road Vehicle Policy, Hoosier National Forest (2350) of July 14, 1972 as supplied to this society by U.S. Department of Agriculture Forest Service.
Out of app. 160,000 acres of land in National Hoosier Forest the Forest Service proposes to open app. 99,000 acres to ORV trail use, while only 62,000 acres would remain closed. The initial cost for these trails would be anywhere between 0500,000.00 to 01,000,000.00 with the maintenance cost 050,000.00 per year and administrative cost 025,000.00 to 050,000.00 per year. This would benefit with the exception of a few independent users, almost exclusively the app. 1000 nembers of the Indiana Motorcycle Association. The beneficiaries (the major interest group manipulating the INA for opening up the national forest to ORV use) are the manufacturers and sellers of motorcycles—for the most part Japanese made.
